MILES CITY. NJ. T., March 49, 1879.


Little VOLTS band of Cheyennes. who have for
over two months been a terror to settlers between
Camp Sheridan and the Yellowstone Valley. have at
last been compelled to surrender. They have trav-
ersed the country i. from the time of their
escape, running Off stock and killing the
lonely travellers the plains until last Tuesday,
whom. almost starving and naked and hard pressed
by the troops sent out from Fort Keogh to intercept
them. they surrendered Lieutenant w. p. Clarke,
Second cavalry. who drove them from the Little
Missouri River to Box Elder Creek and took them
captves securing their and $50 head of ponies


EXPERIENCE OF SCOUTS.


Two Sioux scouts and one half breed sent out
some days previous the capture by Clarke from
days out. ran into the Cheyenne village. numbering
some thirty lodges and situated on tributary of the
Little Missouri eighty miles from Clarkes camp They
captured and held over night by Little Wolf.
tion with the soldiers and were only out on hunt
ing trip, they were released next morning. where
upon they made all possible haste back to Clarke.
giving him the information they had gained at SO
much risk.


THE TROOPS PURSUIT.


They arrived at half-past three O'Clock p NJ. and
at half-past four o'clock the same evening Clarke
and his gallant little band of eighty in the
saddle aud away. They travelled all night and next
day. and the night following rested but few hours
when the march was resumed. and next morning
the place where the village had been To-
Gated was reached. but the Indians. perhaps
repentng Of their haste in releasing the scouts and
thinking all not well. had already flown and
struck out toward the head of Cabin Creek. which
they intended following down to the mouth and
there crossing the Yellowstone. that being the best
fording point between here and Buford.


THE INDIANS ourwITrEp.


Clarke. however, foresaw their intentions and sent
. scout direct to General Whistler at Fort Keogh.
stely ordered one company from Captain snydcr's
command. at .Glendivc. to tho objective point.
and sent from Fort Kcogh seventy five
men. under Leutenants O'Brien and Bailey.
who marched all night and struck Cabin Greek next
day st point thirty miles above its mouth. thus
placing the hostiles between two fires.
THE SURRENDER


They no sooner learned of this new movement
than they crossed over to Box Elder Greek and
were rapidly making for the Big Horn
Mountains. but hotly pursued by
Clarke and his troops that the evening Of
the 9Ssh they realized that they had to fight
render. Knowing Lieutenant Clarke from . former
time when he was stationed among them at their
agency. and that should they show fght at all he
would never let up while of them remained
alive this side Of the line they wisely chose the
latter alternative.


General Whistler. commanding Fort Kcogh, de-
serves great credit for his judicious handling Of
the troops during this campaign.


Lieutenant Clarke. the hero of tho capture is one
of the most dashing officers of the Second cavalry.
He Is brave and energetic and is deserving of great
credit for the subsection Of these Indians The cap
tives expected at Kcogh in few days. when
fuller information may DO obtained.

The Daily Ne,cs, in special edition, pub

Wednesday General Macpherson occupied
Sarkh- Kotal just in time to prevent the junction
of the Kohistanis with force from Ghuznee
The Kohistanis, who occupied position
near the Kotal, were attacked and

of the Fourteenth Bengal Lancers, was to join

den Valley for combined movement, with the
object of driving the enemy south on General
Bakers command.

General Massey encountered Mahmoud JAMS
force, numbering 10000 Afghan Sepoys and
tribemen, and his cavalry made brilliant
charge, but without apparent effect on the vast
body Of the enemy. The country is most diff
cult, being cut up by numerous water courses.
-Four guns, in retiring, were upset, spiked and
abandoned, but were subsequently recovered.
The enemy made for the Cabul gorge, but
were checked there by detachment of the
Seventy-second Highlanders from the Shepur
Cantonment. The enemy then turned toward
Baber's Tomb, and now occupy the heights
south of the Bala-Hissar. They are admirably
1oJ hons of ora

by the cavalry charge and artillery fire, and
never wavered. Our loss is believed to be

enemy. The guides have arrived from Lutta-
bund and General Baker is coming from
Madam. The Times, in its second edition, pub
fishes q shorter version of the same affair. 1t
says:-sThe combined movement of Generals
Massey and Macpherson miscarried. The cavalry
arrived ut the point Of junction too early.
1t encountered large masses of the

ward recovered. The insurgents who are in
considerable force about the city, are being at
tackled this morning by General Macpherson,
who yesterday inflicted severe loss upon them.


THE OFFICIAL ACCOUNT.


The official account of the engagement be-
tween General Massy's command and the force
under Mahomed Jan shows that General
Massey, while attempting to intercept the
enemy, was attacked by great numbers. His
cavalry before abandoning the field overturned
the guns and made repeated charges. The guns
were not recovered until the arrival of General
Macpherson's forces The enemy later attacked
the British in the hills south of the Bala-Hissar

reports that the combination of the tribes against

THE YOUNG BRAVES.


WASHINGTON, d. c., July G, 1870.


letter received at the Interior Department from
DR.. II. Woodbridge, Agency Physician for the Fort
Peck Agency, gives the following graphic description
of the annual "sun dance Of the Sioux nation,
which took place Poplar River in Montana
Territory, about two weeks ago:-


have just witnessed the great Indian festival of
the '.sun dance or worship of the sun. Great
preparations had been made for it and everything
the grandest scale. The city of lodges
moved and the Indians encamped on a beautiful
plain enclosing hollow square large enough for the
movements of thousands of horsemen. In the
centre the great pavilion or medicine lodge
erected, 150 feet in diameter the outside formed of
small posts of green poplar and willow. thickly in
terwoven with green branches. Resting on this and
on a rude framework within, all around for about
twenty feet the space covered with buffalo skins,
forming the dress circle with places assigned to
musicians and actors or dancers. In the centre
the great medicine pole, fifty feet high. The diameter
of the central space--about one hundred feet--was
open to the broad sunlight. Only the men occupied
the deep circle whore they feasted during the
performs nee OF twenty gh continuous hours dur
ing which time about forty dogs were inundated and
eaten, besides large quantities of buffalo meat wild
turnip heads and hot cauldrons OF other eatables
that nameless. The audience was composed of
about five thousand Indians. but MS only the men
occupied the circle within. the common people.
women and boys had to be satisfied by viewing the
performances through the wide entrance through
the nterstices in the leafy barriers All had their
holiday attire the dresses of some OF the chiefs and
those acting directors or priests were gorgeous.


THE DANcERs-ToRrURKs INFLICTED


When all prepared, amid the waving of ban
ners, music and the loud shouting OF the assembled
throng, fifty braves entered. each an Apollo,
painted and naked to the waist, except protusion
of ornaments, with headdresses of beautiful
feathers. their black. glossy hair reaching down
their lower garments. which were most beautifully
and artistcallv arranged Each carried III his hand
ornamental whistle made from the bone of
eagles wing. which was blown shriliy during the
dancing. Each also carried bouquet. composed
mostly of the wild sage. Their appearance and
ccption were grand and imposing. The first after
Moons performance would have been called won
dcrful for display of heroism and power to en-
dure and suffer. Many had from fifty to
two hundred pieces cut out of the living
flesh from their arms and back. The dance
kept up all night with unabated fcrvor. every per-
formance having something new and startling But
in the morning torture rcigned supreme, men
dancing with two, three and four buffalo heads sus
pended from holes cut in their flesh. One Indian
dragged the ground eight buffalo heads fastened
to the flesh of his back aud in the STOPPING posture
ho was forced to assume they had lacerated torn
the cuts in his back to the extent OF three inches
Others held by four different cords two in the
breast and two in tho back fastened to four stakes
and still others were fastened to the centre pole with
ropes which were fastened TO the breast and back.


HoRHfD PICTURE.


Some In addition TO being fastened by the flesh of
their breasts. had buffalo heads suspended from tho
back aud they would be seized by the hanging heads
and jerked until one would think their life would
be forfeited Others made frantic efforts to break
loose, and often noticed the integument to he
stretched three or four inches from the body some
fell faint and exhausted, and. with wild shouts the
din of music and weird songs. made of il perfect
pandemonium. The dancers neither took food, sleep
water during the festival. Their dancing their
invocatons and their prayers were fervcnt They
laid their faces the buffalo heads while praying
for success in hunting. and the priest wep and asked
the Great Spirit to give them In the chase
and let them have food for their wives aud chdren
also to give them plenty OF horses to prosper them
and help them to subduo their enemies. The sod
was carefully removed in spot four feet square,
and within a white spot was made. This is all they
knew, aud with no teacher but nature must Judge
them chariably. Count not impossible that which
seems unlike" Their liberalty was unbounded.
Over two hundred horses were given away, besides
great quantities of other articles.

The WEATHER.-As predicted in Yesterdays
HERALD, "a large depression advanced from the
southwestern districts toward the central val
lcys. Its influence is felt over all the territory
west Of the Mississippi, from the Gulf of Mexico
to Manitoba, and there indications that it
will develop two distinct centres of disturbance.
one in the Northern Missouri Valley and the
other over the Western Gulf States. The area
Of high barometer that extended over all the
northwestern section of the country during the
past few days has moved into the upper lake
regions and Canada, and now dominates the
weather in the districts lying between the Mis-
souri, and st. Lawrence valleys northward of
Ohio, Illinois and Iowa. The area of relatively
high pressure that was over the South At
lantic States has recedcd into the ocean. and the
barometer is now below the mean in that dis
trict. Very little rain fell during the past
twenty four hours, mainly on the South Atlantic
coast and in the New England States. The
weather elsewhere was generally fair, except in
the West, where cloudiness increased toward
night. The temperature varied very little ex-
ccpt over the lakes, where il fell decidedly, and
west of the Mississippi, where it is rising
steadily. The winds have been from fresh to
brisk in the Northwest and West, fresh over the
lakes, the Middle Atlantic and New Eng
laud coast and init elsewhere. The gradients
are likely to become steep in the Missouri and
Mississippi valleys during the next twenty
four hours consequently increasing winds may
be expected. The weather over the British
Islands has improved very much, the pressure
is increasing and the sky is clear. The weather
IN New York and its vicinity today will be
a iphtl, warmer and fair, followed toward night
~ increasing cloudiness. Tomorrow il prom
iscs to be warmer and partly cloudy or fair,
with showers toward night

The power OF Congress to regulate Interstate

right Congressman Reagan, Of Texas, proposes
to have the government establish some regula

passed the House OF the 4jth Congress, but was
buried In the Senate committee. 1t was fought

who are always opposed to any law, except such

of railway matters. The Reagan bill forblds
unjust Determinations by railroads In freight
charges, requires that uniform rates shall be

Two OF the most marvellous specimens Of the
genus homo have been discovered In Morgan
county, KY. They are two boys named James
and Henry Elan, aged respectively eight and
twelve years. These boys talk nationally, are
ordinarily intelligent, but are peculiar In hav-
ing no hair on their bodies and heads. Their
skin is covered with heavy scales like fish. At
the elbow, knees and foot joints the skin is very
thick, resembling the skin OF an alligator. They
never perspire, but turn right blue when they
get heated. They take to water as naturally
as fish, but, strange to say, can't swim. They
dive and crawl along the bottom with great
activity and delight. They cannot walk
bare footed, their feet cracking open, and
have to wear shoes all the time. Their
eyes are large and round, not almond-shaped and
the lids are very red. They never wink, and
sleep with their eyes wide open, and are always
in motion when asleep. Their features are said
to be very good and regular. They have to keep
their bodies greesed when not In the water.
When the body becomes dry the skin cracks
open. Their heads are covered with scales In
lieu OF hair. The boys handle snakes with i'm
punity and delight, frequently quarreling over a
single reptile, but satisfied when each has one,
and snakes have no anttpathy to them, but fol-
low them like dog does his master. The mother
OF these monStrOSit1eS has borne eight children.
The eldest, daughter of sixteen, Is beautiful OF
form and features. and the other children are
not at all peculiar. She cannot account for Ma
lures freak In these cases. They are expected

AARON BURR MAN?

meant to counterfeit the arstocratic Society of

In order to be Enthusiastically native American the

Soon after the society was organized about thirty

RAwLLNs, Oct So A. NJ.


News of the most cheering character has just
been received here from the Indian country.
Captain Paynes surrounded command at Milk
River has been reinforced, both by General
Merritt and Captain Dodge's company Of
colored cavalry, which was supposed to have
been cut off and destroyed. This intelligence,
although in advance of official information, is
accompanied by full particulars. which are Of
the most reassuring nature. General Merritt
reached the vicinity of Payne's camp Monday
forenoon. He defeated the Indians with great
slaughter and without losing man, Monday
afternoon. He brought relief to the corralled
forces about nightfall, shortly after they had
been joined by Captain Dodge and his colored
company from another direction.


HOW THE NEWS WAS BROUGHT.


This important information is brought to this
place by William Humphrey, the mail carrier
from Snake River, point eighty miles distant.
He left Snake River ut ten o'clock yesterday
(Tuesday). William Lithy, one of Merritts
scouts had just arrived at Snake River, having
Monday night.


DECOYING THE INDIANS.


Lirhy reports that General Merritt, Oh his
approach to Payne's camp and when only few
miles from it, discovered hostile Utes filing out
from the neighboring canyons. The Indians
discovered Merritt ut the same moment, and
the General, perceiving this from their
actions, ordered his men to fall back in rapid
retreat. The Indians were encouraged by this
manGuvrc to rush from their hiding places, and
Merritt, pushing his troops to run, drew them
out ON the open plain He then gave the order
to wheel, which the men did with admirable
precision, showing in minutes space a
bristling front, where before had been SEEM
ING struggling rout


VICTORY OVER THE UTEs.


The General did not wait for the foe to attack.
In less than two minutes his men poured into
the Utcs fire which checked their advance
and forced them to seek every available cover
The battle, which began Monday afternoon,
lasted but few hours, during which
time the Indians suffered % loss of thirty
seven killed, while Merritt did not lose
q man. In fact the Utcs got such a severe
drubbing that they threw up white flag in
token Of their wish for parley. This was
granted by General Merritt, and several chiefs
entered his camp forthwith. Several Of the
chiefs were willing to surrender others were
not.


FARLEY WITH THE INDIANS.


Merritt told them that if they would give up

Saratoga had good water for the oarsmen
yesterday after all. and there were not q
few surprises, especially for the Eastern
oarsmen. Pilkington, the New York police
man, was nowhere; little Rathbone gave o
good account of himself, as usual; the
famous Yates, Courtney's old double-scull
partner, failed to show; the redoubtable
Wah-wah-sums Of the Northwest were en-
tirely routed by the Olympics Of Albany,
while the plucky Dauntless boys twice
scored defeat at the hands of the sturdy
Mutuals, both of them, however, disposing
of the Boston "Shawmuts." The Cornell
crew must have been completely disguised
at having actually no crew to compete
with-a curious comment on our college
racing and by contrast recalling vividly
to mind her brilliant work in 1875, when,
on this same Saratoga water, she led twelve
college crews all down the home mile and
crossed the finish line unquestionably the
fastest student crew in America. Clearly,
though however unjustly, there is never
much interest in American college racing
unless Harvard and Yale are on hand.
To-day more fast teams will settle their
relative superiority, and the finale on the
morrow promises plenty of stubborn fight
ing all along the line, and, with good water,
doubtless some very fast time.

The owners of the steamer Borussia allege
that they believe that tho vessel is still af0at,
as she is built with water tight compartments,
and that she is still in the track of American
vessels; they also allege that they are hopeful
concerning the crew and passengers. The third
officers boat was the last to leave the ship.
Among the other boats was a large boat
containing twenty Spaniards, and the mates
boat containing thirteen persons; these
when last seen-prcsumably by the third
officers boat-were doing well. The third
officer made an unsuccessful attempt to tow
another boat containing two men. The crew
Of the steamer, when the boats left, were build
ing rafts. The wind was then blowing
gallo. Later advices by telegraph from Liver
pool represent that nothing really new concern
ing the disaster can be obtained. It is asserted
ut the Office Of the agents that the captain did
his duty manfully.


STORY OF THE THIRD OFFICER.


In his statement the third officer of the BO-
russia says that after the large boat, containing
twenty Spaniards, and the mates boat, contain
ing thirteen persons, had left tho Borussia
lifeboat, containing two of the stewards of the
steamer got adrift. He was sent after this
boat by the captain and took charge of it, TAX
ing his own boat in which five men were left,
in tow; but the boat was swamped and all
on board were drowned. The third Off
Ger endeavorcd to again reach the Bo-
russia, which was fast sinking, but was
unable to make head against the wind.
He was ultimately compelled to abandon the
attempt and run before the wind. At the time
this occurred there were still three boats with
the Borussia. The agents ut Liverpool of the
lost steamer Borussia state that there were one
cabin and sixty-four steerage passengers from
Liverpool for New Orleans and eighty steerage
passengers from Corunna for Havana. A
steamtug which has just arrived at Liverpool
reports that she spoke an inward bound bark
with five more survivors of the steamer Borus-
sin disaster on board. The name of the bark
was not obtained by the tug. She was spoken
off the Saltee Islands.


ADRIFr FOR FIVE DAYS.


Later in the day the bark Fuda arrived at
Liverpool with Ave Spaniards who were saved
from the Borussia. Owing to their inability to
speak English 1t is difficult to get from them
connected narrative of the terrible hardships
they have undergone. Their boat before it
left the Borussia, contained, besides the
Spaniards, the mate and three women but no
sooner was the boat lowered than it was partly
stove by knocking against the steamer. The
mate and the women accordingly returned to the
wreck, but the Spaniards partly stanched the
hole in the boat with some clothes, and their
rope breaking they were cast off from the
steamer. They had some provisions, but none
of them knew anything of scamanship. For
five days and six nights they were tossed about,
suffering terribly, when they were observed by
the German bark Fulda, in latitude 33 deg. 10
min. north, longitude 25 deg. 45 min. west.
They know nothing of the fate of the Borussia.
The latter was conveying to Texas sixty.fve
farmers and their families from the counties of
Lancashire, Yorkshire and Durham and fcw
from Scotland and Ireland.


AN OFFICIAL INQUIRY.


The Board Of Trade has ordered an inquiry
into the loss of the Borussia. The date of be-
ginning the inquiry has not yet been
fixed The Times despatch from Liverpool
says the captain of the Fulda reports that on
the 7th inst he picked up boat, in which
were five Spaniards. The rescued men slept
unintcrruptedly for sixty-cight hours. Upon
being questioned they stated that they had
joined the Borussia Mt Corunna They also
stated that the captain of the Borussia gave the
order to lower the boats. They report that they
stopped the hole in their boat with o pair of
oilslin trousers.

ured on the shore
